premises.text: Industrial robotic arms are expensive, hard to use, and not safe enough for broader non-factory applications
premises.evidence_span: they're expensive, they're difficult to use, and quite frankly, not that safe

premises.text: Cassie delivers industrial-arm capabilities at roughly laptop price (~10× cheaper), with precision motion in a meter envelope and swappable end attachments
premises.evidence_span: Casio has the capabilities of an industrial arm, but the price of a laptop

premises.text: Training is by guiding the arm through motions or using simple app/device interfaces without needing advanced degrees
premises.evidence_span: We've made Casio incredibly easy to train

premises.text: Built-in proximity sensing on every surface detects humans from any point on the arm to make operation around people safer
premises.evidence_span: It can detect a human up to 20 inches away in any direction from any point on the arm

premises.text: Positioned as a developer platform with APIs that let web-level programmers code for the arm across many applications
premises.evidence_span: we've made Cassia a developer platform

value.text: Robotic arms become personal, ubiquitous tools beyond factories
value.evidence_span: make robotic arms as ubiquitous as computers

causal_links.evidence_span: robotic arms can be used for so much more
if you can build a website, you can code for Cassia

notes: Transcript ends mid-sentence at launch CTA; coded only present content (quality.truncated=true). Expense/difficulty/safety folded as one barrier premise (v1.5.1 §4.1.6). Specs, carbon-fiber/muscles, and attachments folded into the cheap industrial-capability product; train-by-demo and proximity skin kept as separately emphasized ease and safety modules within the hardware domain. Biomedical/wheelchair/maker application stories treated as uses of the same democratized arm (fold per §4.1.2), not separate premises. 800 applications treated as traction evidence for the developer-platform condition. ASR name variants Casio/Cassia/Cassie left in spans; normalized to Cassie in premise text.
